Introduction and Study Context Myanmar has experienced ongoing armed conflict since 1948, following its independence from the United Kingdom. Dominated primarily by ethnic-based struggles for self-determination between various Ethnic Armed Organisations (EAOs) and the national armed forces (the Tatmadaw), the situation entered a critical new phase following the February 2021 military coup. The overthrow of the democratically elected government led by the National League for Democracy triggered widespread civil unrest, which rapidly escalated into nationwide armed resistance. Today, Myanmar represents one of the world's most complex and prolonged civil conflicts, characterised by fragmented territorial control, massive civilian displacement and persistent political violence. Conflict is neither spatially random nor static. Peace-building and humanitarian actors need to know where violence clusters, which townships behave unusually relative to their neighbours, and whether clusters are emerging, intensifying or fading. ## 2. Research Objectives and Questions ### 2.1 Research Objectives This exercise uses the Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) Project's records for Myanmar and the MIMU township boundaries to: - Aggregate political-violence events to townships and build a township × quarter space-time cube. - Use **Local Measures of Spatial Association (LMSA)**, specifically Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA), to identify spatial clusters (High-High, Low-Low) and outliers (High-Low, Low-High), and Getis-Ord Gi\* to identify hot spots and cold spots. - Use **Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA)**, which combines time-series Gi\* with the Mann-Kendall trend test, to reveal where, how fast and in what pattern armed conflict is evolving. - Identify where civilians are most exposed to **military air strikes**, whether that exposure is tied to front lines, and where the relatively safer areas are, combining the results into a protection map. ### 2.2 Research Questions - **RQ1:** Where are the statistically significant hot spots and cold spots of armed conflict, and do they differ by type? - **RQ2:** Which townships are spatial outliers, e.g., a violent township surrounded by calm ones? - **RQ3:** Where, how fast and in what pattern has armed conflict evolved between Q1 2021 and Q3 2025? - **RQ4:** Where are civilians most exposed to military air strikes, is that exposure tied to front lines, and where are the relatively safer areas? ### 2.3 Variables The analysis uses event counts of armed conflict as the primary variable, measuring how often armed conflict occurs in each township and quarter. Fatalities are introduced only in the value-added analysis, where the objective is civilian protection. There, the number of deaths per event identifies which forms of attack are most lethal to civilians, and this determines the variable analysed in the rest of that section. Fatalities are not used in the LMSA and EHSA because they are highly concentrated in a small number of mass-casualty events, which would let single incidents dominate a township's results. | Section | Analysis | Variables | Objective | |------------------|-------------------|------------------|------------------| | Data wrangling | Point map, choropleths, space-time cube | `conflict_events`, `battles`, `remote`, `vac` | Map the geographic distribution of conflict | | LMSA | Local Indicators of Spatial Association | `conflict_events`, `battles`, `remote`, `vac` | Hot spots, cold spots and spatial outliers | | EHSA | Emerging hot spot analysis with Mann-Kendall trend | `conflict_events`, `battles`, `remote`, `vac` | Where, how fast and in what pattern violence is evolving | | Value-added | Lethality check; EHSA; bivariate LISA; protection map | `fatalities`, `mil_air`, `clash` | Civilian protection and peace-building | ## 3. "Insurgency", "… $ timestamp 1754410549, 1753971383, 1753971383, 1753971383, 178… ``` ::: ::: ## 4. Data Wrangling ### 4.1 CRS Transformation Myanmar spans roughly 92°E–101°E and straddles UTM zones 46N and 47N, so no single UTM zone covers it without distortion. WGS 84 / UTM zone 47N (EPSG:32647) is used, which contains most townships. The analysis relies on the fields `ST` (state/region), `DT` (district), `TS` (township name) and `TS_PCODE` (unique township P-code). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mmr_ts <- mmr_ts_raw %>% select(ST, DT, TS, TS_PCODE) %>% st_transform(32647) ``` ::: ### 4.2 Fixing townships and centroids #### 4.2.1 Multi-part townships A township may be made of several separate pieces of land, which may lead to two problems: - **The same township stored as several rows.** Every township must be exactly one row, so that it is one location in the space-time cube. We therefore merge rows by `TS_PCODE`. If each `TS_PCODE` only has one row, this changes nothing. - **One row holding many polygon parts.** All parts for mapping and assigning events were kept, so events on islands are still counted. But the centroid of a multi-part township can land in a water body or outside the township, which matters for distance-based analysis. ::: callout-note ### AI Use Disclosure AI tools were used to draft the R code for reducing the dataframe such that there is only one row for every unique combination of `ST`, `DT`, `TS` and `TS_PCODE` before performing a spatial union using *summarise()*, and to find townships with more than one part `n_parts`. The output was reviewed and run by the author to verify correctness against the study data. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mmr_ts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(TS_PCODE) %>% filter(n > 1) #check for rows that share the same TS_PCODE ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TS_PCODE n <0 rows> (or 0-length row.names) ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mmr_ts <- mmr_ts %>% group_by(ST, DT, TS, TS_PCODE) %>% summarise(.groups = "drop") %>% st_cast("MULTIPOLYGON") %>% arrange(TS_PCODE) nrow(mmr_ts) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 330 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} ts_parts <- mmr_ts %>% st_cast("POLYGON", warn = FALSE) %>% mutate(part_km2 = as.numeric(st_area(geometry)) / 1e6) #find the largest piece in kilometres square ts_parts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% count(TS_PCODE, name = "n_parts") %>% summarise(townships = n(), multipart_townships = sum(n_parts > 1), total_parts = sum(n_parts), max_parts = max(n_parts)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 4 townships multipart_townships total_parts max_parts 1 330 41 906 159 ``` ::: ::: Based on the results, there are 41 multi-part townships with 906 pieces in total. The most fragmented township has 159 pieces. What has been addressed: - One row per township: the duplicate check returns no rows, and the merge keeps 330 townships, one row per TS_PCODE. Each township is therefore a single location in the space-time cube. - All pieces kept: the merged townships remain multi-polygons, so every island and detached piece is used for mapping and for assigning ACLED events. No events are lost. #### 4.2.2 Centroids that fall outside boundary *st_centroid* is used to compute the geometric center. *st_intersects()* is used to build a table using `ts_centroid` and `mmr_ts` to test TRUE/FALSE for each centroid against the township using *sparse = FALSE*, while *diag()* was used to ensure that the comparison is made for each centroid with its own township by comparing the values diagonally down the table. *filter(!centroid_inside)* returns a list of centroid that does not fall within the township. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ts_centroid <- st_centroid(st_geometry(mmr_ts)) centroid_inside <- diag(st_intersects(ts_centroid, mmr_ts, sparse = FALSE)) mmr_ts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% filter(!centroid_inside) %>% select(ST, DT, TS) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 8 × 3 ST DT TS 1 Kayah Loikaw Demoso 2 Sagaing Kawlin Kawlin 3 Mandalay Kyaukse Kyaukse 4 Rakhine Sittwe Rathedaung 5 Rakhine Kyaukpyu Kyaukpyu 6 Yangon Yangon (South) Cocokyun 7 Ayeyarwady Labutta Labutta 8 Ayeyarwady Pyapon Pyapon ``` ::: ::: These eight townships indicated under `TS` have a centroid outside their own boundary, such as in a water body or in another township. This would impact any distance-based neighbour analysis. Hence, for each township we take its largest land part and use `st_point_on_surface()` on that part. The result, which we call the anchor point, will then lie on land inside the township's main body. Geometric centroids can fall outside their parent polygon, whereas point-on-surface operations guarantee a point inside it (Lovelace, et al., 2026). For multi-part areal units, Pebesma and Bivand (2023) represent each unit by its largest polygon. This approach combines the two ideas by using a point on the surface of each township's largest land part. ::: callout-note ### AI Use Disclosure AI tools were used to draft the R code that reorders the anchor points to match the township layer using *match()* on `TS_PCODE` and the *stopifnot()* checks that confirm the township codes are in identical order and that every anchor point falls inside the township boundaries. The output was reviewed and run by the author to verify correctness against the study data. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ts_anchor <- ts_parts %>% #build anchor points group_by(TS_PCODE) %>% slice_max(part_km2, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE) %>% #keep only the largest piece in each township ungroup() %>% st_point_on_surface() %>% #compute point guaranteed to be inside polygon select(TS_PCODE) ts_anchor <- ts_anchor[match(mmr_ts$TS_PCODE, ts_anchor$TS_PCODE), ] stopifnot(identical(ts_anchor$TS_PCODE, mmr_ts$TS_PCODE), all(diag(st_intersects(ts_anchor, mmr_ts, sparse = FALSE)))) ``` ::: The following plot is used to show the shifting of the original centroid (red) to the anchor point (blue). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} off_centroid <- which(!centroid_inside) anchor_maps <- lapply(off_centroid, function(i) { tm_shape(mmr_ts[i, ]) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey90", col = "grey40") + tm_shape(st_sf(geometry = ts_centroid[i])) + tm_dots(fill = "red", size = 0.6) + tm_shape(ts_anchor[i, ]) + tm_dots(fill = "blue", size = 0.6) + tm_title(mmr_ts$TS[i], size = 0.9) + tm_layout(frame = FALSE) }) tmap_arrange(anchor_maps, ncol = 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-Home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-8-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: The study boundary is then plotted for checking. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tm_shape(mmr_ts) + tm_borders(col = "grey60", lwd = 0.3) + tm_shape(ts_anchor) + tm_dots(fill = "blue", size = 0.1) + tm_title("Anchor points of Myanmar townships", position = tm_pos_out("center", "top")) + tm_layout(frame = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-Home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: Anchor points appear clustered at certain areas, where townships are much smaller. The densely packed anchor points would be taken into consideration when selecting spatial weighing in ection 6.1. #### 4.2.3 Study Area After cleaning up the multi-part town and centroid issues, the study area is plotted for visual check. ::: callout-note ### Note When the map was first written with older tmap arguments (`style = "cat"` and `palette = "brewer.set3"`), tmap 4 converted them automatically. The conversion added a **"Missing"** category to the legend, even though every township has a state/region value. The code was therefore rewritten in native tmap 4 syntax: `fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical()` and `fill.legend = tm_legend()`. This removes the false "Missing" entry. In addition, the 12-colour Brewer *Set3* palette was stretched with `colorRampPalette()` to give one distinct colour for each of the 18 states/regions. Otherwise colours would repeat and some neighbouring states would share a colour. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mmr_st <- mmr_ts %>% group_by(ST) %>% summarise(.groups = "drop") n_st <- n_distinct(mmr_ts$ST) st_cols <- colorRampPalette(RColorBrewer::brewer.pal(12, "Set3"))(n_st) tm_shape(mmr_ts) + tm_polygons(fill = "ST", fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = st_cols), fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "State / Region")) + tm_shape(mmr_st) + tm_borders(col = "grey20", lwd = 1) + tm_title("Myanmar townships by State / Region (n = 330)") + tm_compass(position = c("right", "top")) + tm_scalebar(position = c("right", "bottom")) + tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE, legend.outside.position = "right") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-Home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){width=768} ::: ::: ### 4.3 ACLED Events ACLED distinguishes three `disorder_type`s, i.e., **Political violence**, **Demonstrations** and **Strategic developments**. *count()* is used to compute the occurrence of the ACLED events and *kable()* is used to generate a table to visualise the variables for further analysis. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} acled_raw %>% count(disorder_type, event_type, sort = TRUE) %>% kable(caption = "ACLED events by disorder and event type") %>% kable_styling(full_width = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
ACLED events by disorder and event type
disorder_type event_type n
Political violence Explosions/Remote violence 22925
Political violence Battles 21121
Strategic developments Strategic developments 17833
Demonstrations Protests 14942
Political violence Violence against civilians 9958
Political violence; Demonstrations Protests 261
Demonstrations Riots 45
Political violence Riots 24
````` ::: ::: After reviewing the data, events whose `disorder_type` contains **"Political violence"** were retained for analysis: - **Battles** (armed clashes, territorial changes); - **Explosions/Remote violence** (air/drone strikes, shelling, IEDs); - **Violence against civilians (**attacks, abductions and sexual violence targeting unarmed people). The following three categories were excluded: - **Riots coded as political violence** (24 events), and the 261 protests coded as **"Political violence; Demonstrations"** (i.e., protests met with lethal force), which reflect civil unrest rather than armed conflict. - **Strategic developments** (17,833 events), such as arrests, looting and base establishment. These are not violent clashes in themselves and are recorded far less consistently. - **Demonstrations** (14,987 events), comprising protests and riots not coded as political violence. These measure civil resistance rather than armed conflict. | Field | Role in this study | |-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------| | `disorder_type` | **Violence variable**: used to select political violence | | `event_type` | **Armed-conflict variable**: Battles, Explosions/Remote violence, Violence against civilians | | `sub_event_type` | Finer breakdown of `event_type` (e.g. Armed clash, Air/drone strike), used in the value-added analysis | | `admin1` / `admin2` / `admin3` | State / district / township (used only to cross-check the spatial join) | | `latitude` / `longitude` | Village-level location, used for plotting and for assigning events to townships | ### 4.4 Data Quality Check `acled_raw` contains two data-quality fields, `geo_precision` and `time_precision`, each coded 1 to 3, where 1 is the most precise. The two fields are independent, where an event can have an exact date but only an approximate location. The interpretation is based on `notes`. - **`geo_precision`**: 1 = the exact town or village is known; 2 = only an approximate location is known (e.g. "near" a town, or within a township/district), so the event is placed at the nearest named location; 3 = only the state/region is known, so the event is placed at a point representing that state/region. - **`time_precision`**: 1 = the exact date is known; 2 = only the week is known; 3 = only the month is known. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} acled_raw %>% count(time_precision) %>% mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 3 time_precision n pct 1 1 82691 94.9 2 2 4212 4.8 3 3 206 0.2 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} acled_raw %>% count(geo_precision) %>% mutate(pct = round(100 * n / sum(n), 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 3 geo_precision n pct 1 1 49261 56.6 2 2 37464 43 3 3 384 0.4 ``` ::: ::: Events with `geo_precision = 3` (about 0.4%) are dropped. Their coordinates mark a state/region rather than the actual location, so assigning them to whichever township contains that point would create artificial hot spots. Events with code 2 are kept, as they are usually located in or next to the correct township. All `time_precision` codes are kept as the time unit used in subsequent analysis is the quarter of the year. ### 4.5 Data Filtering Only conflict events mentioned in Section 4.3 are retained, and events located only to the state/region (`geo_precision = 3`) are excluded. This leaves **53,910 events** from the original 87,109. Two columns are also added: - `qtr`, the quarter in which each event occurred, used to construct the space-time cube; and - `modality`, which distinguishes air/drone strikes and armed clashes from other forms of violence for the trend charts. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} conflict_types <- c("Battles", "Explosions/Remote violence", "Violence against civilians") acled_ac <- acled_raw %>% filter(event_type %in% conflict_types, geo_precision < 3) %>% mutate( qtr = floor_date(event_date, unit = "quarter"), modality = case_when( sub_event_type == "Air/drone strike" ~ "Air/drone strike", sub_event_type == "Armed clash" ~ "Armed clash", event_type == "Explosions/Remote violence" ~ "Other remote violence", event_type == "Violence against civilians" ~ "Violence against civilians", TRUE ~ "Other" ) ) c(raw = nrow(acled_raw), kept = nrow(acled_ac)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` raw kept 87109 53910 ``` ::: ::: ### 4.6 Convert to sf object The `latitude` and `longitude` values from the ACLED dataset are used rather than the ACLED's `admin3` text. The township names in `admin3` have different spellings, e.g., *Hpa-An / Hpaan*, which would result in events being accidentally dropped if identified by township names. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} acled_sf <- acled_ac %>% st_as_sf(coords = c("longitude", "latitude"), crs = 4326, remove = FALSE) %>% st_transform(32647) ``` ::: ### 4.7 Event locations ACLED records each event at the most precise location available, named in the `location` field. Where the exact place is known, this may be a village, which sits below the township in Myanmar's administrative hierarchy. Where only the township is known, the event is placed at the township's main town. Among events with `geo_precision = 1`, there are those with `location` different from their township in `admin3`, i.e., they are recorded more precisely than the township level (ADM3) on which this study is based. The events are therefore first plotted as points, to show their distribution, before being aggregated to townships for the analysis. The selected events, except for political violence: riots which makes up just 24 events, are plotted for viewing. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tm_shape(mmr_ts) + tm_polygons(fill = "grey97", col = "grey75", lwd = 0.2) + tm_shape(mmr_st) + tm_borders(col = "grey40", lwd = 0.6) + tm_shape(acled_sf %>% filter(event_type %in% c("Battles", "Explosions/Remote violence", "Violence against civilians"))) + tm_dots(fill = "event_type", fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = c("#1b9e77", "#d95f02", "#7570b3")), fill.legend = tm_legend(show = FALSE), fill_alpha = 0.25, size = 0.05) + tm_facets(by = "event_type", nrow = 1, free.coords = FALSE) + tm_layout(frame = FALSE, panel.label.bg.color = "white") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-Home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-16-1.png){width=1152} ::: ::: ### 4.8 Point-in-polygon join Events are assigned to townships using *st_join* to check which township polygon each point falls inside, and attaches that township’s TS_PCODE, TS and ST to the event. *left = TRUE* keeps events that fall in no township, with empty (NA) township fields, so they can be counted in the next line. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} acled_ts <- st_join(acled_sf, mmr_ts %>% select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST), join = st_intersects, left = TRUE) unmatched <- acled_ts %>% filter(is.na(TS_PCODE)) nrow(unmatched) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 11 ``` ::: ::: Using *nrow(unmatched)*, 11 points were found to fall outside the township polygons. ACLED's `admin3` field, which records the township ACLED attributes each event to, is used to assign these points instead: - Events with an `admin3` value are matched to values in `TS`. There were eight of such events. - Events with no `admin3` value or values that do not match `TS` values are dropped. There were three of such events. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} reassigned <- unmatched %>% select(-TS_PCODE, -TS, -ST) %>% inner_join(mmr_ts %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% select(TS_PCODE, TS, ST), by = c("admin3" = "TS"), keep = TRUE) acled_ts <- bind_rows(acled_ts %>% filter(!is.na(TS_PCODE)), reassigned) %>% distinct(event_id_cnty, .keep_all = TRUE) nrow(reassigned) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nrow(acled_ts) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 53907 ``` ::: ::: This leaves **53,907 events**. ### 4.9 Township-level aggregates The conflict variables are derived for each township: | Variable | Definition | |----------------|----------------------------------------------| | `conflict_events` | All political-violence events | | `battles` | ACLED event type *Battles* | | `remote` | *Explosions/Remote violence* | | `vac` | *Violence against civilians* | | `clash` | Sub-event *Armed clash* (used in the value-added analysis) | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} acled_df <- acled_ts %>% st_drop_geometry() agg_vars <- function(d) { d %>% summarise( conflict_events = n(), battles = sum(event_type == "Battles"), remote = sum(event_type == "Explosions/Remote violence"), vac = sum(event_type == "Violence against civilians"), clash = sum(modality == "Armed clash"), .groups = "drop") } ts_total <- acled_df %>% group_by(TS_PCODE) %>% agg_vars() # Local Measures of Spatial Association (LMSA) ### 6.1 Spatial weights Comparing the four methods for spatial weights, i.e., polygon contiguity, fixed distance, inverse distance and k-nearest neighbours (KNN), KNN is effective when wanting to ensure a minimum number of neighbours based on geographic proximity and in handling skewed values (as shown in Section 5.1). It is also not sensitive to polygons differing in size, where Myanmar's township ranges greatly, as with polygon contiguity. The use of KNN ensures that every township has neighbours, including the island townships which are located far from the mainland townships and do not share boundaries. Anchor points are dense in Yangon, Mandalay and Nay Pyi Taw, where urban townships are very small (median about 9 km² in Yangon versus about 1,519 km² nationally). A fixed distance band would give these townships dozens of neighbours and leave large rural townships with very few. The k-nearest-neighbour approach gives every township exactly eight neighbours, regardless of township size. Four approaches to defining neighbours were considered, i.e., polygon contiguity, fixed distance, inverse distance and k-nearest neighbours (KNN). KNN was chosen for the reasons below: - Township sizes vary widely. Contiguity works best when polygons are of similar size, and a fixed distance band would give urban townships dozens of neighbours and rural townships very few. KNN gives every township exactly k neighbours, regardless of size. - Every township needs neighbours. Island townships share no boundary with the mainland and would be left without neighbours under contiguity. KNN always finds the k closest townships, so no township is excluded from the analysis. - The conflict counts are highly skewed (Section 5.1). Considering the skewed data, the variables should be evaluated in the context of at least eight neighbours (Modeling Spatial relationships—ArcGIS Pro \| Documentation, n.d.). k = 8 will therefore be used for the weight matrix analysis. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nb_knn <- st_knn(ts_anchor, k = 8) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} nb_lines <- spdep::nb2lines(nb_knn, coords = st_coordinates(ts_anchor), proj4string = st_crs(mmr_ts)$wkt) %>% st_as_sf() tm_shape(mmr_ts) + tm_borders(col = "grey75", lwd = 0.4) + tm_shape(nb_lines) + tm_lines(col = "steelblue", lwd = 0.4) + tm_shape(ts_anchor) + tm_dots(fill = "grey20", size = 0.05) + tm_layout(frame = FALSE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-Home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The plot shows the linking of eight neighbours to each township, including the island township that does not share a boundary with any other township. ### 6.2 Weight Schemes The same k = 8 nearest-neighbour list is used for the weight matrix analysis, with row-standardised weights. Local Moran’s I uses it as is, so each township’s spatial lag is the average of its eight neighbours. Gi\* (in the Gi\* map and in EHSA) requires each township to be part of its own neighbourhood, so *include_self()* is added. | Analysis | Neighbours | Weights | Rationale | |------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------| | Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) | k = 8 nearest neighbours | Row-standardised (`W`) | Spatial lag = average of the eight neighbours | | EHSA (Gi\* per quarter) | k = 8 nearest neighbours **including self** | Row-standardised (`W`) | Gi\* includes the focal township (location i) in its own neighbourhood | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} conflict_w <- conflict_ts %>% mutate(nb = nb_knn, wt = st_weights(nb, style = "W"), .before = 1) ``` ::: ### 6.3 Local Indicators of Spatial Association (LISA) LISA measures, for each township, how similar its value is to those of its neighbours. It identifies clusters, where a township and its neighbours have similar values, and spatial outliers, where a township differs sharply from its neighbours. This is done by computing the local Moran’s I with *local_moran()*. Based on the local Moran's I value, outliers and clusters can be identified: - Outlier: Negative if focal township (location i) is associated with relatively low values in surrounding location (location j). - Cluster: Positive if focal township (location i) is associated with relatively high values in the surrounding locations (location j). In either case, the p-value must be small enough for the cluster or outlier to be considered statistically significant. This report uses α = 0.05, as required by the assignment brief. ### 6.4 Calculating Local Moran's I *lisa* is first created as a function to calculate local Moran's I value with nsim = 99. This will be used for all armed conflicts and the three event types, i.e., battles, explosions / remote violence, and violence against civilians. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lisa <- function(d, var, nsim = 99) { d %>% mutate(local_moran = local_moran(.data[[var]], nb, wt, nsim = nsim), .before = 1) %>% unnest(local_moran) } ``` ::: Local Moran’s I is first computed using `conflict_events`, which looks at total number of armed conflict events per township. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} set.seed(267) lisa_ce <- lisa(conflict_w, "conflict_events") ``` ::: *classify_lisa* is a function created to sieve out townships where results are statistically insignificant, i.e., *p_ii_sim \< 0.05*. This ensures that townships are assigned into a quadrant of High-High, Low-Low, Low-High or High-Low, only if the results are statistically significant, where p value is < 0.05. A Moran scatterplot is plotted to show how the LISA classes arise. Each point is a township, where the x-axis is its standardised number of armed-conflict events, and the y-axis is the spatial lag, the average standardised value of its eight nearest neighbours. The slope of the fitted line equals the global Moran’s I, so an upward slope indicates positive spatial autocorrelation. Townships significant at p < 0.05 are coloured by their LISA class while the rest are shown in grey. The scatterplot complements the LISA mapby showing how strongly each township and its neighbours depart from the mean. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lisa_colours <- c("High-High" = "#d7191c", "Low-Low" = "#2c7bb6", "Low-High" = "#abd9e9", "High-Low" = "#fdae61", "Not significant" = "grey92") classify_lisa <- function(l) { l %>% mutate( lisa_class = if_else(p_ii_sim < 0.05, as.character(mean), "Not significant"), lisa_class = factor(lisa_class, levels = names(lisa_colours))) } lisa_ce <- classify_lisa(lisa_ce) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lisa_ce <- lisa_ce %>% mutate(z_events = as.vector(scale(conflict_events)), z_lag_events = st_lag(z_events, nb, wt), .before = 1) ggplot(data = lisa_ce, aes(x = z_events, y = z_lag_events, color = lisa_class)) + geom_point(size = 2) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "black") + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, lty = 2) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2) + scale_color_manual(values = lisa_colours) + labs(x = "Standardised armed-conflict events", y = "Spatial lag of standardised events", color = "LISA (p < 0.05)", title = "Moran scatterplot: armed-conflict events") + theme_minimal() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-Home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-34-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: The fitted line slopes upward, confirming that armed conflict is positively spatially autocorrelated as townships tend to resemble their neighbours. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lisa_ce %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% summarise(sig_p05 = sum(p_ii_sim < 0.05)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 1 × 1 sig_p05 1 104 ``` ::: ::: There are 108 townships that has a statistically significant local Moran's I value. ### 6.5 LISA Map for Armed Conflict Events The function *map_lisa()* draws the significant classes in colour and greys out non-significant townships, so that only significant results are displayed. State/region boundaries are added for reference. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} map_lisa <- function(l, title) { tm_shape(l) + tm_polygons(fill = "lisa_class", fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(values = lisa_colours, levels.drop = FALSE), fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "LISA (p < 0.05)"), col = "grey60", lwd = 0.2) + tm_shape(mmr_st) + tm_borders(col = "grey25", lwd = 0.6) + tm_title(title) + tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE, legend.outside.position = "right") } ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} map_lisa(lisa_ce, "LISA clusters & outliers: political violence") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-Home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-37-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: ::: callout-note ### Analysis The LISA map reveals a strongly polarised conflict geography. Value-Added Analysis: Protecting Civilians from Air Attacks From late 2023 onward, the military lost territory on the ground and relied increasingly on **air and drone strikes**. The chart compares, per quarter, the number of armed clashes with the number of air/drone strikes, split into those by the military and those by other actors. The dashed line marks the launch of Operation 1027 on 27 October 2023, when the Brotherhood Alliance of three ethnic armed organisations launched a coordinated offensive in northern Shan State. Within weeks it captured more than 100 military positions and several towns on the border with China, and it prompted other resistance groups to launch offensives elsewhere. It was the military’s most serious battlefield challenge in at least three decades (Michaels, 2023). The chart shows whether the military’s use of air power changed after this turning point. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} acled_df %>% filter(modality %in% c("Air/drone strike", "Armed clash")) %>% mutate(series = case_when( modality == "Armed clash" ~ "Armed clashes", inter1 == "State forces" ~ "Military air/drone strikes", TRUE ~ "Other actors' air/drone strikes")) %>% count(qtr, series) %>% ggplot(aes(qtr, n, colour = series)) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + geom_point() + geom_vline(xintercept = as.Date("2023-10-01"), linetype = "dashed") + annotate("text", x = as.Date("2023-10-01"), y = 800, hjust = -0.05, label = "Operation 1027\n(27 Oct 2023)", size = 3) + scale_colour_manual(values = c("Armed clashes" = "#1b9e77", "Military air/drone strikes" = "#d95f02", "Other actors' air/drone strikes" = "#7570b3")) + scale_x_date(date_breaks = "6 months", date_labels = "%Y-%m") + labs(x = NULL, y = "Events per quarter", colour = NULL) + theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](Take-Home_Ex02_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-57-1.png){width=864} ::: ::: Based on the line chart, armed clashes rose sharply after the 2021 coup, from about 150 in the first quarter of 2021 to over 1,000 per quarter by 2022, and peaked at about 1,600 in the quarter Operation 1027 was launched. Since then, clashes have eased to about 1,100–1,300 per quarter. Military air/drone strikes followed a different path. They stayed below about 200 per quarter until mid-2023, roughly tripled to about 430 in the quarter of Operation 1027, and then kept rising, reaching about 840 in the second quarter of 2025. Air strikes therefore grew from about one-tenth of the number of armed clashes in 2022 to roughly three-quarters by 2025, even as ground fighting declined. Other actors’ air/drone strikes grew steadily to a peak of about 340 in early 2024 and have since fallen to about 50 per quarter. The military now carries out most of the air and drone strikes recorded. Together, the trends suggest a shift in how the conflict is fought: after losing ground from late 2023, the military has relied increasingly on air power rather than ground operations. This sets up the value-added analysis, which examines where these strikes fall and what they mean for civilian protection. ## References ACLED.
